Content:
By considering either of the [MATH: 45^\circ] angles in this triangle, we find that
[MATH: \eqalign{
\sin 45^\circ &= \dfrac{\textrm{opp.}}{\textrm{hyp.}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, \[5pt]
\cos 45^\circ &= \dfrac{\textrm{adj.}}{\textrm{hyp.}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, \[5pt]
\tan 45^\circ &= \dfrac{\textrm{opp.}}{\textrm{adj.}} = \dfrac{1}{1} = 1.
}]

Isosceles right triangles are very common, so the values above occur a lot in trigonometry. It's a good idea to remember them.

items.title: Evaluating Trigonometric Expressions With 45 Degree Angles

sections.normalized_html: Evaluate [MATH: 2 \tan{45^\circ} - 4 \sin{45^\circ}.]
EXPLANATION

The angle [MATH: 45^\circ] is special, and its trigonometric ratios have the values

[MATH: \sin{45^\circ} = \dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2}, \qquad \tan{45^\circ} = 1.]

Therefore,

[MATH: 2\tan 45^{∘} − 4\sin 45^{∘}|=; 2(1) − 4((sqrt(2))/(2))|=; 2 − 2sqrt(2)|=; 2(1 − sqrt(2))|.]

Now, we can calculate some trigonometric ratios without a calculator. Let's start with the [MATH: 30^\circ]-angle. By the definition of sine, cosine, and tangent, we have
[MATH: \sin 30^{∘}|= (opp.)/(hyp.) = (1)/(2),; \cos 30^{∘}|= (adj.)/(hyp.) = (sqrt(3))/(2),; \tan 30^{∘}|= (opp.)/(adj.) = (1)/(sqrt(3)) = (sqrt(3))/(3).]

items.title: Evaluating Trigonometric Expressions With 30 and 60 Degree Angles

sections.normalized_html: Evaluate [MATH: \sin{30^\circ} + \cos{60^\circ} + \tan^2{30^\circ}.]
EXPLANATION

The angles [MATH: 30^\circ] and [MATH: 60^\circ] are special angles, and their trigonometric ratios have the particular values

[MATH: \sin{30^\circ} = \dfrac{1}{2}, \qquad \cos 60^\circ = \dfrac{1}{2} , \qquad \tan{30^\circ} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.]

Also, note that [MATH: \tan^2{30^\circ}] simply means [MATH: (\tan{30^\circ})^2.]

Therefore,

[MATH: \sin 30^{∘} + \cos 60^{∘} + \tan^{2} 30^{∘}|=; \sin 30^{∘} + \cos 60^{∘} + (\tan 30^{∘})^{2}|=; (1)/(2) + (1)/(2) + ((sqrt(3))/(3))^{2}|=; 1 + (3)/(9)|=; 1 + (1)/(3)|=; (4)/(3)|.]

Content:
As the angle [MATH: \theta] gets closer and closer to zero, the opposite side [MATH: AC] also approaches zero. Also, the hypotenuse [MATH: BC] and the adjacent side [MATH: AB] become nearly the same length.

Content:
So, as [MATH: \theta] approaches zero (which we can write as [MATH: \theta \rightarrow 0^\circ]) we have

Content:
[MATH: AC \approx 0 \quad \text{and} \quad BC \approx AB.]

Content:
Therefore, when [MATH: \theta = 0^\circ] we have:

Content:
[MATH: \sin (0^{∘})|= (AC)/(BC) = 0,; \cos (0^{∘})|= (AB)/(BC) = 1,; \tan (0^{∘})|= (AC)/(AB) = 0.]

Item 15 — Tutorial: Special Values of the 90 Degree Angle

Content:
The values of the trigonometric ratios for [MATH: 90^\circ] angles are the following:

Content:
| Trigonometric ratio | Value |
| [MATH: \sin \left(90^\circ\right)] | [MATH: 1] |
| [MATH: \cos \left(90^\circ\right)] | [MATH: 0] |
| [MATH: \tan \left(90^\circ\right)] | Undefined |

Content:
To understand where the values come from, this time, we can imagine increasing the value of the angle [MATH: \theta] by moving the vertex [MATH: B] towards [MATH: A.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/67a597a67a3a9915743eb20363e63ab0]

Content:
As [MATH: B] moves towards [MATH: A,] the adjacent side [MATH: AB] gets very close to zero, and the angle [MATH: \theta] gets very close to [MATH: 90^\circ.] Also, the hypotenuse [MATH: BC] and the opposite side [MATH: AC] become nearly the same length.

Content:
So, as [MATH: \theta] approaches [MATH: 90^\circ] (which we can write as [MATH: \theta \rightarrow 90^\circ]) we have

Content:
[MATH: AB \approx 0 \quad \text{and} \quad BC \approx AC.]

Content:
Therefore, when [MATH: \theta = 90^\circ,] we have:

Content:
[MATH: \sin (90^{∘})|= (AC)/(BC) = 1,; \cos (90^{∘})|= (AB)/(BC) = 0,; \tan (90^{∘})|= (AC)/(AB) = (AC)/(0) = undefined.]

Content:
Note that when calculating the tangent, we get a [MATH: 0] in the denominator. We know that we can't divide by zero. Therefore, the tangent of a right angle is said to be undefined.
